lead: Light is a wave, and this unit shows what that wave does at a boundary, in a thin film, at an edge and through a grating. You will learn why soap bubbles show colours, how Newton's rings measure the curve of a lens, and how a grating splits white light into a spectrum. After this unit you can solve the standard interference and diffraction problems and explain how a Michelson interferometer or an anti-reflection coating works.
about: Chapter 4.1 begins with one boundary: reflection, refraction and the phase change that decides every thin-film result later. Chapter 4.2 puts two such waves together to get the bright and dark fringe conditions and applies them to a thin film. Chapter 4.3 bends the film into a wedge and a curved air gap, so counting fringes measures thickness and radius of curvature. Chapter 4.4 does the same job with a Michelson interferometer, and Chapter 4.5 uses a quarter-wave film to cancel reflection. Chapter 4.6 moves from two waves to many wavelets, giving the single slit and the diffraction grating. Chapter 4.7 closes with polarization: light's electric field has a direction, and that direction can be controlled.

chapters.idea: At a boundary light splits into a reflected wave and a refracted wave, and the split depends on the two refractive indices.
chapters.depth: Wavefront and ray; Huygens' construction in one line only. Laws of reflection and refraction; refractive index n = c/v with c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s; Snell's law n₁ sin i = n₂ sin r, angles measured from the normal. Total internal reflection and critical angle sin C = 1/n, named as the idea behind optical fibres. Normal-incidence coefficients: reflectance R = ((n₁ − n₂)/(n₁ + n₂))² and transmittance T = 1 − R. The π phase change when light reflects from a denser medium, because every later chapter depends on it. Name Brewster's angle here, work it in 4.7. Some syllabi call this 'reflection and refraction of EM waves'.

chapters.example: A ray in air (n₁ = 1.00) hits a glass surface (n₂ = 1.50) at 30° to the normal. Find the angle of refraction and the reflectance at normal incidence. sin r = (1.00/1.50) × sin 30° = 0.333, so r = 19.5°. At normal incidence R = ((1.00 − 1.50)/(1.00 + 1.50))² = (−0.20)² = 0.04: 4% of the light reflects and 96% is transmitted.
chapters.trap: Reflection at a denser medium adds a π phase change; forget it and every thin-film answer in 4.2 and 4.5 flips. Also measure i and r from the normal, not from the glass surface.
chapters.prereq: Unit 3, electromagnetic waves and uniform plane waves.
chapters.leave: Polarization by reflection and Brewster's law → 4.7. Total internal reflection inside fibres → Unit 5. Full oblique-incidence Fresnel equations → not needed.

chapters.idea: Two coherent waves added point by point give a steady pattern of bright and dark fringes, set by their path difference.
chapters.depth: Coherent sources and the conditions for sustained interference. Path difference Δ, phase difference δ = (2π/λ)Δ. Resultant intensity I = I₁ + I₂ + 2√(I₁I₂) cos δ; with I₁ = I₂ = I₀ this is I = 2I₀(1 + cos δ). Maxima at Δ = mλ and minima at Δ = (2m + 1)λ/2, m = 0, ±1, ±2. Young's double slit: fringe width β = λD/d, with D the slit-to-screen distance and d the slit separation. Thin film of thickness t and index μ, light at angle r inside: path difference 2μt cos r; the single reversed reflection adds λ/2. Reflected maxima: 2μt cos r = (2m + 1)λ/2; reflected minima: 2μt cos r = mλ. In transmitted light the two conditions swap. Some books write (2m − 1)λ/2 for maxima; it is the same set of odd multiples.

figure.aria: Intensity against phase difference: bright peaks of 4 units at δ = 0, 2π and 4π, with dark zeros halfway between, at π and 3π.

chapters.example: Young's double slit: λ = 600 nm, slit separation d = 1.0 mm, screen distance D = 1.0 m. Fringe width β = λD/d = (600 × 10⁻⁹ × 1.0)/(1.0 × 10⁻³) = 6.0 × 10⁻⁴ m = 0.60 mm. The third bright fringe sits at 3β = 1.80 mm from the centre.
chapters.trap: The extra λ/2 in the thin-film condition comes only from one reversed reflection. Using 2μt = mλ for the bright reflected fringe is the most common error, and so is dropping cos r and taking t alone.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 4.1 for reflection at a boundary and the phase change.
chapters.leave: Wedge and ring geometry → 4.3. Michelson fringes → 4.4. Quarter-wave coatings → 4.5. Many-wave superposition → 4.6.

chapters.idea: A film whose thickness changes steadily turns fringe counting into a ruler for micrometre gaps and lens curvatures.
chapters.depth: Air wedge: two glass plates touching at one edge, separated by a spacer at the other, wedge angle θ in radians. Thickness at distance x from the contact edge is t = xθ. Dark fringes at 2t = mλ, so fringe width β = λ/(2θ) for an air film and β = λ/(2μθ) with a liquid. Spacer thickness: d = Lλ/(2β), with L the plate length and β the measured fringe width. Newton's rings: a plano-convex lens of radius R on a flat plate, air gap t = r²/(2R). Dark rings in reflected light: D_m² = 4mRλ; bright rings: D_m² = 2(2m − 1)Rλ. Centre is dark. Radius of curvature R = (D_m² − D_n²)/(4(m − n)λ), diameters in metres. With a liquid of index μ the rings shrink and R stays the same. Note the ring diameter grows as √m.

figure.aria: Ring diameter plotted against ring number: it grows as the square root of m, from 1.1 mm for the first dark ring to 3.5 mm for the tenth.

chapters.example: Newton's rings in reflected light of λ = 589.3 nm: the 5th and 15th dark rings have diameters 3.0 mm and 4.6 mm. R = (D₁₅² − D₅²)/(4 × (15 − 5) × λ) = (21.16 − 9.00) × 10⁻⁶/(4 × 10 × 589.3 × 10⁻⁹) = 12.16 × 10⁻⁶/2.357 × 10⁻⁵ = 0.516 m, about 0.52 m. The first dark ring then has D₁ = √(4 × 1 × 0.516 × 589.3 × 10⁻⁹) = 1.10 mm.
chapters.trap: The centre is dark, so m = 0 is the dark spot and the first dark ring is m = 1. Mixing radius into a formula written for diameter, or mixing mm with metres, loses the whole mark.

chapters.idea: Split one beam into two paths and recombine it: every fringe that crosses the field is half a wavelength of mirror movement.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this; keep it short. Construction: source, half-silvered plate at 45°, fixed mirror M₁, movable mirror M₂ on a micrometer, compensating plate of the same glass and thickness. The virtual image M₂′ of M₂ forms an air film with M₁, so the instrument is a thin-film experiment with t = d, the mirror separation. Path difference 2d cos θ, giving circular fringes, with θ the angle of the ray inside the air film. Counting: when M₂ moves by d, N fringes cross and d = Nλ/2. Uses: measuring λ, the thickness of a thin transparent sheet, t = mλ/(2(μ − 1)), and the refractive index of a gas cell. Named after Michelson.

figure.title: Michelson interferometer
figure.aria: Light from the source reaches the half-silvered plate, splits to the fixed mirror and the movable mirror, and the returning beams recombine to give circular fringes at the eye.

chapters.example: The movable mirror M₂ is moved by 0.100 mm and 400 fringes cross the field of view. λ = 2d/N = (2 × 0.100 × 10⁻³)/400 = 5.00 × 10⁻⁷ m = 500 nm.
chapters.trap: The path difference is 2d, not d, because the light goes to the mirror and comes back. Writing d = Nλ instead of d = Nλ/2 is the standard slip.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 4.2 and 4.3 for path difference and fringe counting.

chapters.idea: A film one quarter wavelength thick makes the two reflected waves cancel, so the surface stops reflecting.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this; keep it short. The problem: bare glass (μ = 1.50) reflects about 4% at each surface, which costs light in a camera lens or solar cell. Quarter-wave layer of thickness t = λ/(4μ_f) at the design wavelength. With air above and glass below, both reflections are reversed, so no extra relative phase arises from reflection and cancellation needs 2μ_f t = λ/2. Amplitude reflectance of the layer at normal incidence r = (n₁n_s − n_f²)/(n₁n_s + n_f²), with n₁, n_f, n_s the indices of air, film and substrate. The best index is μ_f = √μ_glass, which gives exactly zero; real materials like MgF₂ come close. Multilayer and broadband coatings, and the uses on lenses, spectacle glass and solar cell covers.

figure.aria: Three layers with light entering from the top: air, then a magnesium fluoride film about 100 nm thick, then glass.

chapters.example: A magnesium fluoride film (μ = 1.38) coats glass of index 1.50, designed for λ = 550 nm. t = λ/(4μ_f) = 550/(4 × 1.38) = 99.6 nm, about 100 nm. The ideal index would be √1.50 = 1.22; with 1.38 the residual reflectance is R = ((1.00 × 1.50 − 1.38²)/(1.00 × 1.50 + 1.38²))² = (0.4044/3.4044)² = 0.014, about 1.4% instead of 4%.
chapters.trap: A single-layer coating is tuned to one wavelength; it does not remove reflection across the whole visible range. Also the phase reversal is at both surfaces here, so the cancellation needs 2μ_f t = λ/2, not the thin-film condition of 4.2 with one reversal.
chapters.leave: Multilayer design equations → outside this book. Film thickness measurement by interference → 4.2 and 4.4.

chapters.idea: Light passing an edge or many narrow slits superposes its own wavelets, giving dark bands where a grating sends different wavelengths to different angles.
chapters.depth: Diffraction against interference: two waves in 4.2, countless wavelets here. Fresnel (near field) and Fraunhofer (far field) named in one line, with the screen far away and plane wavefronts assumed. Single slit of width a: minima at a sin θ = mλ, m = ±1, ±2, …; central maximum angular half-width θ = λ/a and linear width 2Dλ/a on a screen at distance D. Plane transmission grating: slit width a, opaque gap b, grating element d = a + b, N lines per metre. Grating equation d sin θ = mλ. Highest order from sin θ ≤ 1, so m_max = d/λ. Resolving power λ/Δλ = mN_total, with N_total the total number of illuminated lines. Dispersive power dθ/dλ = m/(d cos θ). Uses: spectrometer, wavelength measurement, a CD track acting as a grating.

figure.aria: Relative intensity against β: a tall central peak of height 1 near β = 0, then much smaller side peaks separated by zeros at β = π, 2π and 3π.

chapters.example: A grating has 5000 lines per cm and is used with light of λ = 600 nm. d = 1/(5000 cm⁻¹) = 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ cm = 2.0 × 10⁻⁶ m. First order: sin θ = (600 × 10⁻⁹)/(2.0 × 10⁻⁶) = 0.300, θ = 17.5°. Second order: sin θ = 0.600, θ = 36.9°. Third order: sin θ = 0.900, θ = 64.2°. The fourth needs sin θ = 1.20, so only 3 orders appear.
chapters.trap: For a grating use the grating element d = a + b, never the slit width a; a sin θ = mλ is the single-slit minimum condition. Also check m_max, because an order with sin θ > 1 does not exist.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 4.2 for superposition of two waves.
chapters.leave: Fresnel diffraction integrals and zone plates → outside this syllabus. Detailed grating spectra and absent orders → not needed beyond one mention.

chapters.idea: Light is a transverse wave, so its electric field has a direction, and a polarizer controls how much of it passes.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this; keep it short. Transverse nature shown by the fact that two crossed Polaroids cut the beam to zero. Unpolarized, plane polarized and partially polarized light. Production: by reflection at Brewster's angle tan θ_p = μ, with θ_p measured from the normal (about 56° for glass); by dichroism in a Polaroid or H-sheet; by scattering; by double refraction in calcite, giving ordinary and extraordinary rays and an optic axis, with Nicol prism named only. Malus's law I = I₀ cos²θ, with θ the angle between the polarizer and analyser axes. Quarter-wave and half-wave plates as one line each. Optical activity and a mention of applications: sunglasses, LCD screens, stress analysis.

figure.aria: Transmitted fraction against angle: it falls from 1 at 0° to 0 at 90° and back to 1 at 180°, following cos²θ.

chapters.example: Unpolarized light of intensity 64 W/m² passes through a Polaroid and then a second Polaroid at 60° to the first. First Polaroid: I₁ = 64/2 = 32 W/m². Second: I₂ = I₁ cos²60° = 32 × 0.25 = 8 W/m². For glass of index 1.50 the Brewster angle is θ_p = tan⁻¹(1.50) = 56.3°.
chapters.trap: Unpolarized light loses half its intensity at the first polarizer; skipping that factor of ½ doubles the answer. Keep the angle between the two polarizer axes, and measure Brewster's angle from the normal.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 4.1 for reflection at a boundary; Unit 3 for transverse electromagnetic waves.
chapters.leave: Jones vectors and Stokes parameters → outside this book. Full double-refraction theory → not needed.
